meta.title: Termide — all-in-one terminal workspace for desktops and servers
meta.description: Editor with LSP and a debugger, dual-pane file manager with SFTP/FTP, terminal, git, database viewer, a coding agent that runs on your own model and plugins in any language — one zero-config static binary written in Rust.

homes.title: // Two homes, one tool
homes.subtitle: The same binary and the same keys at your desk and on a box you reached over SSH.

editor.d: Completion, go to definition, references, rename and diagnostics from any language server, seven of them set up out of the box.

debug.d: F5 runs to a breakpoint set with Ctrl+F8; step and read the stack and variables in a debug panel. lldb, GDB, Delve and debugpy; a Python, Go or Rust file needs no setup.

agent.d: Point it at llama.cpp, Ollama or vLLM on your machine and no code leaves it, or use a hosted endpoint.

git.d: Status, a coloured commit graph, diffs, stashes, and branches together with their worktrees.

docs.d: Rendered Markdown, Mermaid diagrams, HTML and images in panels beside the editor.

commands.d: Build, test and deploy commands in commands.toml, per project, on a hotkey, and can run from the project root wherever you are.

static.d: A static musl binary with no OpenSSL and no libc to match: Alpine, ARM boards, containers, Termux.

remote.d: SFTP, FTP and FTPS in the file manager; copy between hosts while the transfer runs in the background.

detach.d: termide --detached keeps editors, shells and jobs running; --attach brings them back at any size.

monitor.d: CPU, memory, network and disk in the menu bar, with top processes and listening ports a click away.

db.d: SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL tables with sorting, filters, cell editing and export.

agent.title: // A coding agent that asks first
agent.subtitle: Describe a task; the model reads, edits and runs commands in your project, and every change waits for your approval.

models.d: Any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoint: llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, omlx or a hosted provider. The context window comes from the server when it reports one. Paste a screenshot into the prompt and the model sees it.

permissions.d: Allow once, for the session or always for a pattern; deny with a reason the model reads; plan mode refuses every write; /undo and checkpoints take edits back.

tools.d: Read, edit, write and shell, plus web search and fetch through a browser profile of its own, never your logins, or over plain HTTP where no browser runs, and recall over earlier sessions, git history and project files, and debug: breakpoints, stepping and evaluation in the same session you watch.

agents.d: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI over the Agent Client Protocol, and your own agents. Hand a task to a copy of the agent or to any of them: it runs out of sight while you watch, take it over or stop it; a pause holds it, and a restart carries it on. Agents in different panels message each other and do not overwrite each other's edits.

autonomy.d: /goal keeps it at a task until a separate judge agrees it is done, /loop repeats a prompt on an interval, and work cut off by a closed panel picks up where it stopped.

extend.d: Skills, prompt templates, command scripts, MCP servers, hooks, plugins and project instructions, all plain files.

visibility.d: Live phase and speed, prefill progress, a context bar and token totals; each answer ends with its time and tokens. Pick the reasoning level per model; sessions resume later.

agent.cli_desc: The same agent, tools and permission rules without the UI:

asks.d: It asks before every change, and /undo takes it back.

others.t: Already on Claude Code or Codex?
others.d: Run them in the same panel.

features.title: // Everything else
features.subtitle: The rest of what ships in the binary.

editor.d: Completion, hover, go to definition, references, rename and quick fixes; a diagnostics panel; tree-sitter highlighting for 23 languages.

debugger.d: Breakpoints beside the line numbers that move with your edits; a debug panel over DAP (lldb-dap, GDB, Delve, debugpy) with the call stack, variables, stepping and expression evaluation; the program gets a terminal of its own for input. Command-line lldb, gdb, dlv and pdb work too.

outline.d: Structural navigation through tree-sitter queries, synced with the cursor.

docs.d: Rendered Markdown and HTML, a text-mode browser that saves pages as Markdown, and Mermaid diagrams drawn as text, including class diagrams from your source.

hex.d: Hex/ASCII view with a byte cursor, selection and search; overwrite editing with a .bak backup.

fm.d: Tree with nested git status, glob and regex search, selection by mask, batch operations, bookmarks and a directory switcher that lists mounted disks. Zip, tar and ISO archives open like folders, also on a server; P packs the selection at the compression level you pick, Alt+F9 unpacks.

remote.d: SFTP, FTP and FTPS in pure Rust; SMB and NFS through the OS mount.

bgops.d: Copy, move, upload and download with progress, pause, resume and cancel.

db.d: SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL: server-side sort, per-column filters, cell editing, rows as TSV, JSON or INSERT.

detach.d: Close the terminal or lose the connection; attach again later from any terminal (Unix).

terminal.d: Full PTY with scrollback, search, mouse and URL detection; the title follows your cd.

monitor.d: CPU, RAM, network and disk; top processes by CPU, memory or connections, with listening ports.

static.d: Linux x86_64 and ARM64 (glibc or musl), macOS, native Windows and Android Termux.

git.d: Status, log with a coloured commit graph, diff, staging, stash, blame, branches and their worktrees; a folder of many checkouts lists them as a tree.

projects.d: Panel layouts restored per directory, with per-project settings and commands; projects you switch away from keep running in the background, one button each in the menu bar.

commands.d: Global or per-project commands with hotkeys, parameter forms and terminal, background or report modes.

palette.d: Ctrl+P fuzzy command palette; Ctrl+G opens a file, a folder or a URL with path suggestions.

plugins.d: A program in any language, copied into plugins/, speaks JSON-RPC: palette commands with keys, status bar items, panels, editor marks, completion and formatting on save, tools for the agent. Each is on, opt-in or off in your global config; a project only switches it within that.

themes.d: Dark, light, retro and cinematic; write your own in TOML.

languages.d: English, Chinese, Russian, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish and more.

keyboard.d: Every binding is editable in Settings; full mouse support; hotkeys work on a Cyrillic layout and with Alt on macOS.

vim.d: Optional Vim-style editing for those whose fingers expect it.

vault.d: Passwords of SFTP, FTP, databases and git live in an encrypted vault under a master password (Argon2 + ChaCha20-Poly1305), never in bookmarks, layouts or logs.

offline.t: Goes only where you point it
offline.d: No telemetry, no update checks: termide connects to the servers, databases and model endpoints you set up, and nothing else.

repo.d: A project's MCP servers, hooks and commands wait for your approval before they first run, and its config and agents cannot name the programs termide starts or loosen the agent's permissions.

prompts.d: The agent's system prompt, service prompts and tool descriptions are plain files you can read and override; /prompt shows the assembled result.

ai.q: Do I have to use the AI agent?
ai.a: No. No provider or model is set by default, so the agent does nothing and sends nothing until you configure one. Everything else works without it.

unattended.a: Yes, within the limits you set. /goal keeps it at a task until a separate judge agrees it is done, /loop repeats a prompt on an interval, and on_limit = "wait" waits out a rate or subscription limit instead of stopping. In the default auto mode a reviewer model decides what your permission rules leave open, so it rarely stops to ask; deny rules hold in every mode.

privacy.a: No telemetry, no account and no update checks. It goes online only when you ask: a remote location, a web page, git push or pull, or a model for the agent.

repo.q: Is it safe to open a repository I just cloned?
repo.a: termide runs nothing a repository brings until you approve it: a project's MCP servers, hooks and commands ask first, plugins come only from your own config directory, and a project's settings cannot change the programs termide starts or loosen the agent's permission rules, only make it ask or refuse more.

tmux.a: For the common case of keeping work alive over SSH, yes: termide --detached keeps the whole workspace running and --attach brings it back. It does not manage arbitrary sessions and windows the way tmux does, and runs fine inside tmux.

ssh.q: How do I use it on a server?
ssh.a: Copy the static musl binary and run it; nothing else needs installing. You can also stay local and open the server over SFTP or FTP from the file manager.

terminals.a: Any modern terminal with true colour. Images are drawn natively in Kitty, WezTerm, iTerm2, Ghostty and foot; Alt hotkeys on macOS work in terminals with the Kitty keyboard protocol.

windows.a: Yes, natively through ConPTY in Windows Terminal, or in WSL. Detached instances are Unix-only.

keys.q: Do I have to learn new keys?
keys.a: Menus list every shortcut, the mouse works everywhere, and the dual-pane layout will feel familiar from mc or FAR. Every binding can be changed in Settings, and there is an optional Vim mode.
